candidates.attacker_control:
The `style` attribute value (and its presence) in submitted HTML, on any element whose tag policy action is `validate` (e.g., `` or `

`). The attribute name is matched case-insensitively via `"style".equalsIgnoreCase(name)`.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The shipped default policy antisamy.xml defines `style` as a global-tag-attribute (line 478), so for that policy both DOM and SAX paths take the CSS branch and there is no visible delta - the bypass matters only for policies without a style definition (shipped slashdot/tinymce variants omit it from globals; slashdot also has no css-rules). The value itself is still passed through CssScanner, so only policy-allowed CSS (or an empty string) is emitted; the style branch is only reachable for tags with action `validate`; I could not prove that the CSS whitelist can be escaped to execute script. The unchecked branch may also be long-standing upstream behavior rather than a regression, which would lower severity.
candidates.impact: Sanitizer policy bypass: HTML that the configured policy explicitly disallows from carrying a `style` attribute is emitted with a style attribute by the default SAX scan path. In policies that intentionally exclude CSS (e.g., the Slashdot policy, documented as allowing no CSS), elements acquire style attributes anyway; with policies that do define css-rules but disallow the style attribute, attacker CSS permitted by those rules (e.g., URL-loading properties, positioning/overlay properties) is applied against policy intent. No script-execution payload was demonstrated from this defect alone, so the direct impact is attribute whitelist bypass / policy-enforcement inconsistency rather than confirmed XSS.
candidates.prerequisites: Application scans with the SAX scanner (the default for `AntiSamy.scan(String)`) and uses a policy that does not put `style` in the tag definition, global-tag-attributes, or dynamic-tag-attributes (for example antisamy-slashdot.xml, which intentionally allows no CSS; or a custom policy that disallows style). If the policy contains css-rules, attacker CSS allowed by those rules is kept; if it has no css-rules, an empty `style=""` attribute is still added.
candidates.root_cause: In MagicSAXFilter.startElement the `style` attribute is special-cased and copied into `validattributes` unconditionally after CSS scanning; the earlier policy lookup (`attribute`) is never consulted for the style case. The DOM implementation instead gated the same branch on `attr != null`, so an element whose policy does not define a `style` attribute (per-tag, global, or dynamic) can still receive a style attribute through the SAX scanner, including an empty one when the policy has no CSS rules.
candidates.title: SAX scanner retains/synthesizes style attribute even when the policy does not allow it (DOM scanner does not)
candidates.trace: AntiSamy.scan() -> AntiSamySAXScanner.scan(String) -> MagicSAXFilter.startElement (line 300 `tag.isAction("validate")`) -> attribute loop builds `attribute` via tag/global/dynamic lookup (lines 312-320) -> the `style` branch (line 322) runs regardless of `attribute == null` -> CssScanner.scanInlineStyle(value, tag, maxInputSize) cleans the CSS -> `validattributes.addAttribute(makeSimpleQname(name), "CDATA", cr.getCleanHTML())` (line 328) -> element is emitted with `super.startElement(element, validattributes, augs)` (line 469), so the style attribute survives. The DOM equivalent (AntiSamyDOMScanner.processAttributes lines 577-598) only enters the CSS branch when `attr != null`; otherwise the attribute is removed by the `attr == null` path (lines 682-696), so the same input/policy yields different output depending on scan type.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and no runtime scan output was produced; the claim that the SAX path is reachable with a style-disallowing policy is based on source reading of shipped policies/custom-policy support, not a live test. Whether maintainers consider this a security defect, and whether any policy/CSS combination escalates it to XSS, was not established.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-284 Improper Access Control / sanitizer whitelist bypass (potential CWE-79 precondition)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 58 repository files (no binaries/symlinks excluded); 26 Java files parsed by the P1 relation index, 4 files absent from the index (consistent with the four largest policy XML files, which I reviewed by targeted text search). I read the full text of all Java source files in src/main/java (AntiSamy, CleanResults, InternalPolicy, Policy, TagMatcher, css/*, html/model/*, html/scan/*, html/util/*) and inspected the shipped policy XMLs (directives, common regexes, style attribute/global attributes, css-rules) across antisamy.xml, antisamy-slashdot.xml, antisamy-tinymce.xml and by cross-policy grep for the URL/selector/URI regexes. No src/test tree is present in the snapshot, the antisamy.xsd referenced for policy schema validation is absent, and no build, tests, scanners, or dependency sources were available or executed. Index capabilities explicitly lack control/data flow and semantic resolution, so reachability statements are syntactic only.
limitations: No runtime verification: findings are based on source reading only; no scan output, test execution, or exploit payload was produced.

The SAX strategy's serializer/transformer behavior (xercesImpl 2.12.2 HTMLSerializer, XSLTC identity transformer) could not be inspected because dependency sources are not in the snapshot; some output-escaping questions (e.g., CDATA handling) remain unverified.
The policy schema file antisamy.xsd is not present, so schema-enforced constraints on policy structure could not be checked.
No test suite is present, so expected-sanitization behavior for the DOM/SAX divergence could not be confirmed against project tests.
Only the shipped policy XMLs were sampled; arbitrary custom policies (which change whether the style attribute is defined and which CSS rules exist) could alter reachability and impact.
The relation index covers only 54 of 58 files and provides navigation hints only; no claim is made that unreported areas were exhaustively audited.

rejected_leads.lead: SSRF in the deprecated remote-stylesheet import path: CssScanner.parseImportedStylesheets validates the @import URI against offsiteURL/onsiteURL and then performs httpClient.execute(new HttpGet(stylesheetUri)) (CssScanner.java lines 247-371, execute at 328).
rejected_leads.reason: Requires the deprecated, non-default policy directive embedStyleSheets=true (false in all shipped policies; CssHandler.importStyle returns early otherwise), is explicitly documented as dangerous/deprecated, and is reachable only through attacker-supplied CSS when that opt-in feature is enabled. Real but config-gated; not the strongest evidence for this review.

rejected_leads.lead: AntiSamyDOMScanner.stripNonValidXMLCharacters only calls replaceAll when the entire input matches the single invalid-character pattern (lines 818-825), so invalid XML chars are not stripped from mixed strings despite the Javadoc/comment.
rejected_leads.reason: Confirmed logic defect against the comment, but no demonstrated security impact: the result (NekoHTML parse failure/DoS or dropped characters) was not traced to a sanitizer bypass, and this pattern may be long-standing upstream code.

rejected_leads.lead: XMLUtil.decode/encode guard each entity replacement with Matcher.matches() (XMLUtil.java lines 154-204), so multi-entity strings are not decoded.
rejected_leads.reason: Used only while parsing the trusted policy XML, not attacker input; no trust-boundary crossing identified.

rejected_leads.lead: Policy.getDynamicAttributeByName matches any attribute whose lowercased name starts with the dynamic key (Policy.java lines 935-945), combined with allowDynamicAttributes=true in the default policy; DOM passes the non-lowercased name while SAX passes the lowercased name.
rejected_leads.reason: Emits only ordinary attributes whose names/values are escaped by the serializer; no attribute-name smuggling or handler injection could be substantiated from source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: CssValidator.validateValue compares allowed literals with allowedValue.equals(value) after lowercasing the input (line 270).
rejected_leads.reason: If policy literals contain uppercase characters this is stricter, not weaker; no bypass follows.

rejected_leads.lead: Property stores neither description nor onInvalid (Property.java lines 50-61), and CSS onInvalid is never used by CssHandler.
rejected_leads.reason: No security behavior depends on these fields in this snapshot; apparent dead data, not an exploitable defect.

summary: Reviewed the AntiSamy 1.7.6-SNAPSHOT source tree (58 files; 26 Java files parsed by the relation index). I traced the two sanitizer pipelines (DOM and SAX) from attacker-controlled HTML/CSS into policy validation and serialization, inspected the CSS scanner/validator/handler, policy parsing and loading, attribute/tag models, entity encoder, URI utilities, and the shipped policy XML regexes. The one concrete, security-relevant divergence I could substantiate is that the SAX scanner emits a (possibly synthesized) `style` attribute even when the active policy does not allow a style attribute for that tag, while the DOM scanner removes it — a sanitizer whitelist/policy bypass in the default scan path. I did not find an evidence-backed path to raw script execution; other suspicious spots (deprecated remote CSS import SSRF, odd Matcher.matches() guards, dynamic-attribute prefix matching) are gated by non-default configuration or lack demonstrable security impact and are listed as rejected/unconfirmed leads.
